sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: No, GTA 6 didn't break the Australian internet, but it sure did break records

stories.headline: GTA 6 rolls out on consoles as Australia's NBN sets a traffic record
stories.dek: Rockstar's rolling midnight launch starts in Oceania, while PC players wait on a version Rockstar has yet to announce.
stories.body:
Grand Theft Auto VI is unlocking around the world in a rolling launch. Rockstar is releasing it at midnight local time on November 19 in each region, which put players in New Zealand's time zone in the game from 6 am Eastern on Wednesday, November 18, according to PC Gamer. It is out on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S only, targeting 30 fps, with no PC release yet.

The download is already straining networks. TechRadar reports the game weighs up to 212GB, and preloading has been live since November 10. NBN Co told TechRadar that Australia's National Broadband Network hit an all-time traffic peak of 33.19Tbps on November 12, the day boxed code versions reached retailers, beating the 2025 record of 32.91Tbps. NBN Co noted a Fortnite patch landed the same day. The company says that was about 3Tbps, or 10 percent, above baseline.

Since preloads opened, NBN Co has recorded more than 70 petabytes of extra traffic, which it calls roughly equal to 330,000 GTA 6 downloads. Not all of it is necessarily Rockstar's doing. Tasmania saw the largest peak increase over its usual baseline, 16.3 percent, while Western Australia saw the smallest at 6.6 percent.

The game arrives with heavy expectations. Newzoo's Emmanuel Rosier told PC Gamer that "without GTA 6 the console market would likely be down year-over-year in 2026," after rising hardware costs dented console sales. GTA 6 is also the most-nominated game at The Game Awards on December 10, with eight nominations including Game of the Year.

The PC version remains unconfirmed. Rockstar has said nothing official, and GTA 5 took a year and a half to reach PC. A GamesBeat report citing five sources says GTA 6 will arrive on PC in the first few months of 2027. Online play is also absent at launch; Twitch's CEO said earlier this year that the online component would launch in 2027.

In a PC Gamer reader poll, 29 percent said they would play at launch rather than wait for PC. Rosier said the game's longer-term story "will depend on what happens next, particularly on PC and online."
key_points: Rolling launch unlocks at midnight local time on November 19 per region
Console-only on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, with a download of up to 212GB
NBN hit a record 33.19Tbps on November 12, with a Fortnite patch also contributing
GamesBeat sources point to a PC release in early 2027, unconfirmed by Rockstar
stories.why_it_matters: PC players still have no official date, though reporting points to early 2027. Anyone buying on console should plan for a download of up to 212GB.

cover.caption: Extra NBN traffic in Australia since GTA 6 preloads began

sources.title: OpenAI just unveiled GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol

stories.headline: OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to paid ChatGPT users
stories.dek: Astra targets complex projects and Sol everyday work; OpenAI claims better benchmark scores at a fraction of the cost per task.
stories.body:
OpenAI has released two new models, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is built for complex projects, Sol for everyday work. Both are available now in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu subscribers, TechRadar reports, and both are coming to the OpenAI API. Free accounts are left out, and the models run only in Work mode, not Chat mode.

OpenAI's pitch is efficiency. The company says both models do better on demanding tasks while using fewer tokens, which stretches usage limits further. On Agents' Last Exam, OpenAI reports GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the estimated API cost per task. It also scored 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic rival Claude Fable 5.2 at 5 percent of the cost, according to OpenAI. These are the company's own figures.

There is a pricing shift too. For the first time, subscribers to the $200-per-month ChatGPT Pro tier get Ultrafast mode with GPT-6.2 Sol. OpenAI says Ultrafast processes requests up to eight times faster than GPT-6 Astra in Standard mode in Codex. It was previously limited to ChatGPT Pro 500 subscribers. Pro 500 users and API developers can use Ultrafast with either model, and eligible Enterprise and Edu users get it once a workspace admin turns it on.

As a showcase, OpenAI developer Thomas Ricouard asked GPT-6.2 to recreate Paris at full scale as a browser world he could walk or drive through. The model combined street maps with French survey data on more than 131,000 buildings, and Ricouard refined the result by feeding it screenshots of what he wanted changed. TechRadar tried the result, called Paris Atlas, and found it slow to load but convincing, with 3D pedestrians to steer around using the arrow keys.

TechRadar's take is that casual users asking questions or drafting emails probably won't notice a difference. The gains matter more for people building websites, tools or apps. OpenAI's announcement topped Hacker News on launch day.
key_points: GPT-6.2 Astra for complex projects, Sol for everyday work
Available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for paid tiers, API coming
OpenAI claims Astra beats Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points at 5% cost
$200 Pro tier gets Ultrafast mode with Sol for the first time
stories.why_it_matters: If OpenAI's cost-per-task claims hold, Codex users and API developers get stronger agentic coding for less money and fewer burned tokens. Free users get nothing new.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak on Java 17+ AVX-512 VBMI Servers

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Critical Java4Shell flaw allows RCE attacks on major Java applications

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Oracle to Patch 11 Java Flaws Today as Critical OpenJDK RCE (CVE-2026-114938) Report Emerges

stories.headline: Java4Shell flaw opens Jira, Jenkins and Keycloak to pre-auth attacks
stories.dek: An OpenJDK Base64 bug on AVX-512 servers allows remote code execution, Calif says. Oracle, Amazon and Azul have patched, but Red Hat has not.
stories.body:
A memory-corruption bug in Java's Base64 decoder lets attackers without an account run code on Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, according to Calif, the security firm that disclosed it on Tuesday. The flaw, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, affects Java 17.0.6 and later, plus Java 21, 25 and 27. It only triggers on x86-64 chips with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake and newer, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 is not affected.

The bug sits in a hardware-accelerated decoder that Java switches to for frequently run code. A malformed string ending in an extra = makes it write 62 or 63 bytes past its output buffer before Java rejects the input. BleepingComputer reports the trigger can be as simple as 64 "A" characters followed by =. Because servers often decode Base64 login headers, SAML artifacts and CSRF tokens before checking authentication, no login is needed. Calif says it also achieved authenticated code execution on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

The overwritten bytes are fixed, which led early analyses by Upwind and Equixly to predict only crashes. Calif says it got around this by corrupting a neighboring array to gain read and write access to memory. There is no universal exploit, and each target needs its own memory layout and timing. Calif is withholding its application exploits. Other labs have reproduced crashes and a memory leak, but not code execution, The Hacker News reports. Canada's Cyber Centre says it knows of no attacks. Calif told BleepingComputer that researcher Quang Luong found the bug in about an hour using OpenAI's Codex, then built a working exploit in two more hours, for under $200 in AI costs.

Severity ratings differ. Calif scores the flaw 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. Red Hat gives it a preliminary 9.8. Amazon rates it 8.8, and Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. Oracle shipped fixes on November 17 in new .1 builds, such as 17.0.21.1 and 21.0.13.1. Amazon Corretto and Azul Zulu are also patched. Red Hat's fixes are still pending, and Temurin, Microsoft's build and Liberica had not listed fixed builds as of The Hacker News' check.

Admins who cannot update yet can start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, or use -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 only. After updating, restart services and rebuild container images.
key_points: CVE-2026-114938 affects Java 17.0.6+, 21, 25 and 27 on AVX-512 VBMI chips
Calif reports pre-auth RCE on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, Confluence and others
Oracle, Corretto and Zulu are patched; Red Hat fixes are still pending
Workaround: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics until a fixed build is installed
stories.why_it_matters: Any Java 17+ service on a recent Xeon or Zen 4 host may be exposed, and the same container image can be safe on one server and vulnerable on another. Update the runtime, rebuild images, or set the JVM flag now.

cover.caption: AI cost to find and exploit Java4Shell, according to Calif

stories.headline: Nvidia board rules out Jensen Huang's return as CEO
stories.dek: Huang said he would be honored to come back after resigning over affairs, but chairman Harvey C. Jones says the board unanimously declined.
stories.body:
Nvidia's board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, chairman Harvey C. Jones said on a regularly scheduled investor call, PC Gamer reports. The statement came hours after Huang posted on X that he would be "honored" to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America.

Huang resigned on November 12 after disclosures of two extramarital affairs. Tom's Hardware reports one was with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive some US intelligence officials believe may be a Chinese government asset, and another with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia vice president who reported directly to him. China has denied the espionage accusation.

Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney and Travis Kalanick backed his return, and President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" it. CFO Colette Kress remains interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.
key_points: Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones says the board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and will not reinstate him.
Huang said he would return as CEO if asked, and apologized for "serious mistakes" in his personal life.
CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and the board has created a national security and export control oversight committee.

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Massive Kik data breach exposes more than 150 million images — experts say popular messaging app may have leaked incredibly sensitive material

stories.headline: Exposed Kik database leaks more than 150 million profile images
stories.dek: Researcher Jeremiah Fowler found images appearing to show child abuse and reported them to NCMEC and Connecticut's attorney general.
stories.body:
An unencrypted, non-password-protected database held just over 150 million Kik profile images uploaded between 2021 and 2026, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler says, TechRadar reports. The files were split into thumbnails and originals, meaning about 75 million were unique full-size photos. They could be viewed in any browser via a Kik-associated subdomain.

In a sample of about 2,000 images, Fowler found 66 that appeared to contain child sexual abuse material. He reported some images to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and the Connecticut Attorney General's office. Kik's terms have required users to be 18 or older since 2025, but Fowler says he saw many people who appeared to be minors.

Kik, owned by MediaLab, locked down the database after disclosure. It did not respond to TechRadar's request for comment, so how long the data was exposed and who may have accessed it remain unknown.
key_points: Exposed database held over 150 million Kik profile images, about 75 million of them originals, uploaded 2021 to 2026.
66 of roughly 2,000 sampled images appeared to contain CSAM; Fowler reported images to NCMEC and Connecticut's attorney general.
The database was secured after disclosure; Kik owner MediaLab did not respond to TechRadar's request for comment.

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it

stories.headline: Microsoft puts Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot
stories.dek: At Ignite, Satya Nadella called Copilot "the new OS for work," with a persistent agent called Copilot Autopilot coming next.
stories.body:
Microsoft has made Word, Excel and PowerPoint generally available inside Copilot, CEO Satya Nadella announced Tuesday in his Ignite keynote. He described Copilot as "the new OS for work." Users can create documents, spreadsheets and presentations directly in Copilot, and the files stay editable in the regular Office apps.

As Ars Technica reports, the move flips the usual model. Agents drive the work, and the apps become plugin components, backed by a knowledge layer that draws on emails, meetings, calendars, chats and files. Microsoft IQ, which houses that Work IQ context layer, is also now generally available.

Next is Copilot Autopilot, which Microsoft calls a "persistent, proactive agent." Users can delegate whole responsibilities to it across services like email and calendar. It will bill per use through Copilot Credits. Final pricing has not been announced.
key_points: Word, Excel and PowerPoint are now generally available inside Copilot, with files still editable in the Office apps.
Microsoft IQ and its Work IQ context layer, which draws on company emails, meetings and chats, are generally available.
Copilot Autopilot, a cloud-based autonomous agent, will use usage-based Copilot Credits billing; pricing is not yet set.

sources.title: Japan takes Fugaku supercomputer offlline after cyberattack

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Japan’s most powerful supercomputer may have been hacked, over 4,000 users’ personal data stolen

stories.headline: RIKEN pulls Fugaku offline after breach exposes 4,222 users
stories.dek: Attackers used Fugaku's public status dashboard to reach internal servers, planting malware that grabbed user data, SSH keys and research files.
stories.body:
RIKEN has taken Japan's Fugaku supercomputer offline after an intruder used its public operational status dashboard to reach multiple internal servers between November 10 and 13. The research institute says names, email addresses and user IDs of 4,222 Fugaku users were compromised, along with names and emails of 375 users of its Rikyu AI supercomputer. SSH private keys, access keys and research data files stored on users' computers were also taken, according to BleepingComputer.

RIKEN says the attacker tried some stolen keys on other systems but found no further unauthorized access or theft of research results. The intrusion method and attacker remain unknown. Fugaku was shut down on November 14, login keys were disabled, and users are told to replace stored credentials and watch for phishing.

Fugaku, a 537-petaflop machine built with Fujitsu, entered shared use in March 2021.
key_points: An intruder exploited Fugaku's public status dashboard between November 10 and 13 to reach internal servers.
Data of 4,222 Fugaku users and 375 Rikyu users was compromised, plus SSH and access keys.
RIKEN shut Fugaku down on November 14 and will restart it only once it is safe.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Cloud keys leaked in Docker Hub images are stolen within seconds

stories.headline: Cloud keys leaked in Docker Hub images get stolen in seconds
stories.dek: Stony Brook researchers planted honeypot credentials in 300 container images and saw the first AWS key abused 7.86 seconds after publication.
stories.body:
Attackers extract and abuse cloud credentials exposed in public Docker Hub images within as little as eight seconds, according to research reported by BleepingComputer. Stony Brook University researchers Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis published 300 honeypot images across eight public registries over four months, seeding them with AWS, OpenAI and Anthropic API keys plus decoy SSH and database credentials.

The fastest AWS key use came 7.86 seconds after publication. The median first API call arrived at 51 seconds, and all 100 AWS keys were used within 15 minutes. The images were pulled more than 75,000 times, and the AWS keys drew over 140,000 API calls from 5,000 IP addresses. Scanners mostly read image layers directly rather than running containers.

The researchers say they reported the findings to Docker in May and received only an acknowledgment. An August check found no changes.
key_points: The fastest observed abuse of a planted AWS key came 7.86 seconds after the image hit Docker Hub; all 100 AWS keys were used within 15 minutes.
Leaked OpenAI and Anthropic keys were quickly used to drain test-account balances.
The researchers urge Docker Hub to scan images for secrets and rate-limit its feed of new images; they say Docker has not acted since May.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Researchers hijack Hugging Face account for popular Kokoro AI model

stories.headline: Researchers hijack Kokoro's Hugging Face account via expired domain
stories.dek: By registering a lapsed domain, a team reset the publisher's password and showed poisoned weights could ship as a routine update.
stories.body:
Security researchers took control of the Hugging Face account behind Kokoro, a popular open-weight text-to-speech model, by registering the developer's lapsed domain and resetting the password, BleepingComputer reports. Kokoro draws nearly 13 million monthly downloads and is supported in tools from Google, Nvidia and Intel, with AMD and AWS publishing guides for it.

The team, led by Alon Hertz, registered hexgrad.com, listed in Kokoro's DONATE.md file. They then fine-tuned the model's weights in 87 seconds on a gaming GPU so it spoke different words than the input text. They tested this locally and never uploaded it. Because only weights change, scanners have no malicious code to detect, the researchers say.

Hertz says Hugging Face does not verify that accounts remain with their original owners. He reported the issue but got no response.
key_points: Researchers registered the lapsed hexgrad.com domain and used it to reset the Kokoro publisher's Hugging Face password.
They altered Kokoro's weights in 87 seconds to produce different speech, testing only locally.
Kokoro has not been updated since April 2025 but still sees nearly 13 million monthly downloads.

featured.headline: Gravity Circuit hits its lowest price ever at €4.24: Strong Buy
featured.body:
Gravity Circuit, a lesser-known 2D action platformer with pixel graphics, is down 75 percent at the IndieGala Store to €4.24 from a regular €16.99. That is the lowest price ever recorded for the indie title. The ratings are the strongest on today's list: Overwhelmingly Positive on Steam and a Metascore of 89.

The deal runs until 00:59 CET on November 24, 2026, which leaves a full week. A deep cut, a record-low price and top-tier reviews add up to a Strong Buy. It suits players who like action platformers and pixel-art indies, and at under €5 it is a low-risk pick for anyone curious about the genre.

opinion.headline: 'No hackers involved' is the alarming part of last week's outages
opinion.dek: Microsoft and US officials offered the absence of attackers as comfort, but mundane changes to concentrated systems deserve the scrutiny now reserved for breaches.
opinion.body:
At 3:36 pm EST on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration stopped departures from every US airport. It was only the third nationwide ground stop in the agency's history, after 9/11 and the 2023 NOTAM outage, and it lasted until 8:35 pm EST. Ars Technica reports that over a million travelers were affected. The trigger, according to Tom's Hardware, citing the Wall Street Journal and FAA statements, was two newly installed HPE Juniper routers: one at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and one at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas.

The comfort came quickly. Homeland Security's Markwayne Mullin said the event "is not a threat to the US" and called it a telecommunications outage, TechRadar reports. Microsoft, apologizing for a global Microsoft 365 outage that began November 12, described it as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents," according to PC Gamer. Both statements are meant to reassure. I think they should do the opposite. If nobody attacked these systems, then ordinary maintenance took them down, and ordinary maintenance happens every day.

Look at what the mundane managed. Microsoft says its failure was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a recent network change. BleepingComputer reports that the company blames a July bug, which triggered a cascading failure that left more than 80 percent of its networking gateway servers unresponsive. Outlook, Teams and Copilot were disrupted. Hospitals, banks, courts and Japan's government were affected, Ars Technica reports. Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News it looked like "one of the biggest outages of all time," possibly worse than recent AWS and CrowdStrike incidents.

The FAA's version is even plainer. The two routers began sending a high volume of data across the agency's communications network. "A thousand connections over every four to five seconds," FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy said. That overwhelmed a decades-old copper network and disrupted contact between controllers and pilots. Staff traced the flood to a specific router feature and disabled it on all Juniper routers. Restoring communications took about four hours. HPE says the routers worked as intended and "did not fail." That line deserves more attention than it got. Nothing was broken, nobody was hostile, and departures still stopped nationwide.

Then there is the pool. WDR reports that 15 guests at Phantasialand's Hotel Ling Bao in Brühl, Germany, were injured after a defective automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the water. Four went to the hospital, and one was kept for observation. The park told the broadcaster its maintenance safety system had raised the alarm by email, and Microsoft's outage on Friday meant the messages never arrived. A hotel pool in Germany turned out to depend on Microsoft's network gateways. That is what concentration means in practice.

The official framing has a fair case behind it. An attack implies an adversary who picked the target and may come back, so ruling one out tells the public what kind of response is needed. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also has a point when he blames decades-old analog equipment and warns there will be "more of these" without major system updates. Nobody can freeze a network. Upgrades are how capacity grows and old gear gets retired. All true, and all of it sharpens the argument. Modernizing means more changes, not fewer, and each new device has to meet the old copper. The copper is old, but the thing that was new was the pair of routers. An attacker has to get in first. An approved change is already inside. My prediction: more of these will arrive during the updates too, unless the updates get the scrutiny a breach would.

Two rules would be a start. First, no safety alarm should have email as its only path. Tom's Hardware argues that safety systems need local or analog backups, and I agree. Second, new hardware should prove itself against the network it will join before it goes live on a critical one. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford says the agency is investigating whether installation, configuration or the hardware itself was at fault. Whatever the answer, a feature capable of flooding the network was live at two sites, and the fix was to switch it off everywhere. Should that discovery have been made with over a million travelers waiting?

Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report, and the FAA's investigation is still open. Watch whether either one says what review the change received before it shipped, not only what broke afterward. Closer to home, list every alert that reaches people through a single channel or a single vendor, and ask what happens when that channel is silent. Then treat the next routine rollout the way a suspicious login gets treated: as something that has to earn trust.
opinion.pull_quote: If nobody attacked these systems, then ordinary maintenance took them down, and ordinary maintenance happens every day.
opinion.thesis: Microsoft and the FAA framed their failures as reassuring because no attackers or AI were involved, but that is the alarming part. A network upgrade, a latent July bug and two new Juniper routers did more damage in a week than most breaches. Mundane changes to concentrated systems deserve the scrutiny now reserved for hackers, starting with no more email-only safety alarms and no untested hardware on critical networks.

fixes.sentence: Microsoft and the FAA offered the absence of attackers as comfort, but mundane changes to concentrated systems deserve the scrutiny now reserved for breaches.
fixes.problem: The reassurance about no attack came from Homeland Security's Markwayne Mullin and other officials, not the FAA.
fixes.replacement: Microsoft and US officials offered the absence of attackers as comfort, but mundane changes to concentrated systems deserve the scrutiny now reserved for breaches.
